metadata.name: Software Development Flow
metadata.description: Task-first software development with source-grounded planning, independent semantic review, impact-based validation, conditional visual reports, accepted-unit VCS checkpoints, and repository-grounded final coverage.
metadata.author: mcp-moira-team

nodes.directive:
Capture the user's development task and authority before task-specific discovery or repository mutation. Read all standing project instructions. Create ./moira-ws/software-development-flow-{task-name}-{YYYYMMDD}-{HHMM}/ and treat it as the new workspace throughout this directive; do not use workspace_path before returning it. In this same turn write the standards this flow works to into standards/ inside that workspace — planning.md from {{planning_standards}}, engineering.md from {{engineering_standards}}, tests.md from {{test_standards}}, documentation.md from {{documentation_standards}} and review.md from {{review_standards}} — so every later responsibility, including a delegated reviewer, reads them there. Inside that workspace, write this execution ID to process-id.txt and keep task-requirements.md as the single canonical requirements source. Resolve every explicitly assigned ticket, pull request, issue, specification, or document through available project-native mechanisms; preserve its identity, retrieval location, and complete current content in durable source files without preliminary relevance filtering, then separately incorporate all authoritative requirements without reducing them to a lossy summary. If a source cannot be obtained, expose that blocker instead of planning without it. Before mutation, inspect project-native VCS read-only and record VCS kind, branch or bookmark, status, relevant diff/baseline, unrelated changes to preserve, and already authorized side effects in vcs-baseline.md without assuming Git or requiring a clean tree. Discover task-relevant entry points, interfaces and data flow, implementations, dependencies and consumers, tests and fixtures, coverage policy/maps, documentation, configuration and schemas, generated artifacts, project-native commands, build/environment/health, runtime/integration surfaces, UI/browser architecture, CI/review/checklists, ownership boundaries, and applicable security/performance constraints. Record exact locations/evidence or a justified N/A in project-context.md. Use additional project-native searches when one search is insufficient; never conclude that an artifact or dependency does not exist from one superficial search. Ask only for a material fact that cannot be discovered. Do not create permanent guides merely because one is absent, and do not mutate the repository here. Return the new workspace path as workspace_path.

Resolve `operating_mode` in this same turn: reuse a mode the user already stated; infer an unambiguous one, including a run started by an already autonomous parent process; otherwise ask once, naming the consequence — in `autonomous` there are no intermediate approvals of requirements, plan, units, or result, only the final report, while `interactive` keeps every current approval. The mode holds for the whole run and is never asked again.
nodes.completionCondition: Task, authority, assigned sources, canonical requirements, read-only VCS baseline, correlated workspace, and relevant project context are durably captured before mutation

nodes.directive: Present the complete current requirements at {{workspace_path}}/task-requirements.md and ask whether they accurately capture the task, constraints, authority, and acceptance criteria. Read the file when exact current content is not already available or may have changed. Do not edit it here. On rejection, save the user's verbatim feedback to {{workspace_path}}/requirements-feedback.md.
nodes.completionCondition: The user approved the current requirements or supplied actionable feedback

nodes.directive: Use the verbatim feedback in {{workspace_path}}/requirements-feedback.md to update {{workspace_path}}/task-requirements.md. Preserve every unaffected requirement and authority boundary, resolve conflicts with the user when necessary, and keep one canonical requirements source. Do not create a parallel summary.
nodes.completionCondition: Canonical requirements incorporate the feedback without losing unaffected requirements

nodes.directive: Determine whether initial project-health evidence is relevant to the approved task. Use project-native instructions and the task-relevant context already captured; a missing guide is not permission to skip applicable checks. When relevant, run the smallest startup and baseline-test checks that establish a truthful starting state. Write {{workspace_path}}/project-health.md with exact commands, outcomes, and classification. Distinguish a healthy state, inapplicability, unrelated pre-existing failure, repository failure that this task must resolve before development, and an external blocker requiring changed state.
nodes.completionCondition: Applicable baseline evidence and a truthful classified outcome exist in project-health.md

nodes.directive:
Present the external blocker from {{workspace_path}}/project-health.md. Ask the user to confirm that external state changed before retrying, or to abort. Do not retry on an unchanged environment. If aborting, ensure the health report contains the current blocker and partial-work facts.

In `autonomous` mode do not ask: re-check the external state yourself and retry only on evidence that it actually changed; otherwise abort with the blocker and partial-work facts recorded.
nodes.completionCondition: The user confirmed changed external state or chose to abort

nodes.directive:
Create the current material plan revision at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md from the canonical requirements, resolved assigned sources, task-relevant project evidence, VCS baseline, and actual repository contracts. Define independently completable outcome-oriented units with affected responsibilities and boundaries, dependencies and ordering, contracts and invariants, observable acceptance evidence, expected task-owned files, applicable tests and coverage-map updates, permanent documentation, security/performance/runtime/UI obligations, risks, and unresolved decisions. Map every affected or at-risk behavior to automated evidence or a justified manual check. Explicitly mark each unit that requires screenshot capture, actual visual inspection, and a self-contained step-report.html; do not infer or add that obligation later merely because a UI file changed. Record the requested project-native authority for checkpoint commits after accepted units and final reconciliation. Preserve executor freedom over exploration, decomposition details, tools, edit order, and repair tactics unless a real external contract constrains them.

Follow `{{workspace_path}}/standards/planning.md`; the path is canonical and unchanged content need not be reread when already present and certain.
nodes.completionCondition: A complete outcome-oriented current plan revision exists with observable evidence, conditional visual-report obligations, and requested VCS authority

nodes.directive:
Review {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md independently against the complete canonical requirements, every assigned primary source, standing project instructions, relevant repository architecture and behavior, VCS/side-effect boundaries, and prior completed work. Use a separate reviewer context or subagent when the host supports it; otherwise perform a fresh self-review and disclose that fallback in the report. Read primary artifacts directly when they are not already available or may have changed. Verify requirements coverage, dependencies, writer/reader contracts, executable routes, test and documentation obligations, task-file ownership, checkpoint authority, and observable evidence. Reject an unjustified omission of screenshot/visual/HTML evidence when the outcome cannot be adequately accepted without it. Overwrite {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/review.md with the findings, as the review standard requires. Do not block on formatting taste, fixed step counts, or speculative redesign. Return only the count of all current blocking findings; zero is valid.

Judge the plan by `{{workspace_path}}/standards/planning.md` and conduct the review by `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`; both paths are canonical and unchanged content need not be reread when already present and certain. A standard that does not apply to this change is met.
nodes.completionCondition: The complete current independent plan review exists, discloses reviewer independence or fallback, and its count matches all blocking findings

nodes.directive:
Repair the current plan revision using {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/review.md. Reproduce each blocking defect, correct the root cause in the plan, preserve still-valid decisions and executor freedom, and update the same plan artifact. Do not implement style suggestions or create review bookkeeping.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/planning.md` and `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: The current plan revision changed to address every reproduced blocking defect

nodes.directive:
Present the complete reviewed plan revision at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md with its architecture, outcomes, dependencies, evidence obligations, conditional visual-report units, risks, and side effects. Ask for explicit plan approval and one explicit project-native VCS authority that covers both checkpoint commits after accepted units and final reconciliation. On approval, derive the next uncompleted 1-based plan-unit index and total unit count from this exact revision and return them with vcs_commits_authorized. On rejection, also save verbatim feedback to {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/user-feedback.md. Do not edit the plan or mutate VCS here.

In `autonomous` mode do not ask for approval: acceptance follows from the independent plan review that already passed. Derive the cursor and unit bound from this exact revision and set VCS authority strictly from the authority captured at task start in {{workspace_path}}/vcs-baseline.md — never grant authority the task did not give.
nodes.completionCondition: The user decision, approved cursor and bound, conditional evidence obligations, and checkpoint/final VCS authority or rejection feedback are durable

nodes.directive:
Write the material plan revision {{plan_revision}} to {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md, from the rejected plan at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{previous_plan_revision}}/plan.md and the verbatim rejection at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{previous_plan_revision}}/user-feedback.md. The engine has already advanced the revision number; do not renumber it. Preserve the rejected revision where it stands, carry forward unaffected requirements and completed work, and do not create a summary relay.

Follow `{{workspace_path}}/standards/planning.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: A new material plan revision incorporates the user's rejection feedback

nodes.directive:
Implement approved plan unit {{current_step_index}} of {{total_steps}} from {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md. Use the complete current plan when not already available or when it may have changed. Own the complete approved outcome: inspect real dependencies and surrounding contracts, change the repository, preserve unrelated work, add or update necessary tests and coverage artifacts, update applicable permanent documentation, and run useful focused checks. Inventory every changed or at-risk behavior and contract and map it to concrete automated evidence or an explicit manual verification reason. Write the unit's account to {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md in this turn. It is the account of the unit, not of your turn: it states what the unit now delivers and the evidence for it — task-owned files, commands and outcomes, behavior/evidence mappings, documentation impact — together with which earlier behaviour of this unit the change could have disturbed, unresolved facts, and unrelated changes that must remain excluded. Carry the decisive output itself instead of prose retelling it. You are its first owner and not its only one: every later responsibility that changes this unit leaves it true, so write the present state rather than the story of this round. Open it with the unit's baseline in one line — the checkpoint of the previous unit where the project's version control provides one, the state in {{workspace_path}}/vcs-baseline.md for the first unit, otherwise the repository state as it stands at the start of this unit — because every later gate and repair of this unit judges against that line. Do not commit or publish here.

Work to `{{workspace_path}}/standards/engineering.md` and `{{workspace_path}}/standards/tests.md`; the paths are canonical and unchanged content need not be reread when already present and certain. Where the surrounding code is wrong, implement correctly, say where you diverged, and report the defect rather than repairing unrelated areas.
nodes.completionCondition: The complete approved unit, dependencies, task-owned changes, tests, docs, behavior inventory, focused evidence, and the current unit account are in place

nodes.directive:
Inspect the actual repository changes for plan unit {{current_step_index}}, standing project instructions, the approved outcome, the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md, the record of the round just closed at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{previous_iteration}}/repair.md when this is not the unit's first pass, and the affected behavior inventory. Run the smallest project-native deterministic checks that diagnose the affected scope; this mechanical gate does not require a separate reviewer context. Explicitly consider formatting, lint, static analysis, scoped type checking or compilation, targeted/unit tests, need for new or changed tests and coverage-map updates, permanent documentation, public contracts, shared schemas/configuration, migrations, concurrency, generated artifacts, infrastructure, and project checklists. For every applicable area provide exact evidence; for every materially plausible omitted area give a concrete N/A reason. Overwrite {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/cheap-validation.md with commands/outcomes and every reproducible repository defect. Do not rerun broad checks whose evidence is current, and do not treat unrelated or external failures as success. Return only the blocking issue count.

The subject is the unit as it now stands against its baseline — the line that opens {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md — not the diff of the latest repair. Rerun what the latest change could have invalidated, leave current the evidence it could not reach, and say which is which.

The linter, the type system and the compiler are what run here; tests are not a substitute for them, and a test that asserts what those tools already guarantee adds maintenance without protection.
nodes.completionCondition: Current independent cheap-validation evidence covers every materially applicable affected area and its issue count matches reproducible repository defects

nodes.directive:
Use the current cheap-validation report to reproduce and repair every repository-caused blocking defect at its root. Preserve unrelated changes and do not absorb unrelated or external failures. Never obtain a pass by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, coverage, or another quality gate; change a validator or test only with concrete proof that its expectation is obsolete. Do not add sleeps, force, blind retries, swallowed errors, suppression, or timeout inflation. Record this correction in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/repair.md, the record of the round you are closing: what you changed, which earlier behaviour of the unit that could have disturbed, and the evidence for the repair itself, added to whatever an earlier correction of this same round already recorded, and run focused evidence before independent revalidation.

When this correction changed the unit, bring the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md to what the unit now is, in this same turn: you are its current owner, so rewrite what your change made untrue rather than appending a section about this round.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: Repository content changed to repair reproduced cheap-validation defects

nodes.directive:
Judge test adequacy yourself from the primary sources, not from your own account of the work: read the actual diff for plan unit {{current_step_index}}, the approved unit, the behavior inventory, the tests themselves, project coverage maps and thresholds, standing test rules, and the current validation evidence. Inspect changed and at-risk behavior, boundaries, contracts, schemas, configuration, integrations, regression risks, concurrency, migrations, and failure paths rather than using function or assertion counts. Verify that tests exercise observable production behavior, would fail on the relevant regression, and are not duplicated across levels without purpose. Overwrite {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/test-adequacy-review.md with the findings, as the review standard requires. Return only the complete issue count; zero is valid.

The subject is the unit's tests as they now stand against the unit's baseline, the line that opens {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md — not the tests this round happened to touch, and not an earlier round's verdict carried forward.

Judge the tests by `{{workspace_path}}/standards/tests.md` and take from `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md` only what applies to any review — the report file and its finding format, that zero findings is valid, and the bar for what blocks; both paths are canonical and unchanged content need not be reread when already present and certain. A standard that does not apply to this change is met. Judge this gate here yourself: do not delegate it and do not obtain a separate reviewer, because the unit's one independent review is the completeness review that follows.
nodes.completionCondition: The test-adequacy gate is judged here from the actual diff, tests and current evidence; it covers changed and at-risk behavior and its count matches the blocking findings in its report

nodes.directive:
Use the current test-adequacy report to reproduce every confirmed gap and repair the production behavior, necessary tests, implementation seams, and coverage maps at their root. Preserve unrelated changes. Never obtain a pass by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, coverage, or another quality gate; change a validator or existing expectation only with concrete proof that it is obsolete. Do not add sleeps, force, blind retries, swallowed errors, suppression, or timeout inflation, and do not absorb unrelated failures. Record this correction in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/repair.md, the record of the round you are closing: what you changed, which earlier behaviour of the unit that could have disturbed, and the evidence for the repair itself, added to whatever an earlier correction of this same round already recorded, and run focused evidence before independent revalidation.

When this correction changed the unit, bring the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md to what the unit now is, in this same turn: you are its current owner, so rewrite what your change made untrue rather than appending a section about this round.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/tests.md` and `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.

After the repair, state its reach as repair_reach: a description of what you actually changed, never of how important the finding was. It is `contained` when the change stayed in the tests, fixtures and coverage artifacts this gate judges, left production behaviour untouched, and the project's own deterministic checks over what you changed have been run and pass. It is `spreading` when it reached production code, contracts, schemas, configuration, dependencies or generated output, or when those checks could not be run or did not pass. A repair that turned out larger than it looked is `spreading` whatever it looked like when you started, because `contained` skips the validation chain and returns straight to this gate — the checks that change could have invalidated would never run.
nodes.completionCondition: Repository content changed to repair all reproduced test-adequacy defects

nodes.directive:
Judge the architecture yourself from the primary sources, not from your own account of the work: read the actual implementation for plan unit {{current_step_index}}, canonical requirements, the approved plan, standing instructions, assigned architectural sources, the surrounding project code, and the current behavior and test evidence. Check conformance with established project and broadly accepted patterns, responsibility separation, cohesion/coupling, dependency direction, contracts and invariants, justified abstractions, extensibility and evidenced scalability, deterministic test seams, maintainability, lifecycle and error handling, plus applicable security/performance/UI concerns. Overwrite {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/architecture-review.md with the findings, as the review standard requires. Set requires_replan only when the approved plan itself cannot produce a correct result, including when newly proven visual acceptance is necessary but the unit lacks the approved screenshot/HTML obligation. Do not constrain implementation with speculative design or aesthetic preference; zero findings is valid.

The subject is the unit's design as it now stands against the unit's baseline, the line that opens {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md. A structure that decayed across repair rounds is this gate's finding even when the latest change was small.

Judge the architecture by `{{workspace_path}}/standards/engineering.md` and take from `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md` only what applies to any review — the report file and its finding format, that zero findings is valid, and the bar for what blocks; both paths are canonical and unchanged content need not be reread when already present and certain. A standard that does not apply to this change is met, and nothing need be produced to prove it inapplicable. Judge this gate here yourself: do not delegate it and do not obtain a separate reviewer, because the unit's one independent review is the completeness review that follows.
nodes.completionCondition: The architecture gate is judged here from the actual implementation and surrounding project code; it is project-grounded and has an accurate issue count and replan decision

nodes.directive:
Use the current architecture review and any current closure feedback to reproduce and repair every confirmed defect that can be resolved within the approved plan. Correct root causes in code, tests, or documentation; preserve valid project patterns and unrelated changes; do not implement speculative suggestions or absorb unrelated failures into task scope. Never obtain a pass by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, architecture constraints, or another quality gate; change a validator or test only with concrete proof that it is obsolete. Do not add sleeps, force, blind retries, swallowed errors, suppression, or timeout inflation. Record this correction in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/repair.md, the record of the round you are closing: what you changed, which earlier behaviour of the unit that could have disturbed, and the evidence for the repair itself, added to whatever an earlier correction of this same round already recorded, and run focused evidence before independent revalidation.

When this correction changed the unit, bring the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md to what the unit now is, in this same turn: you are its current owner, so rewrite what your change made untrue rather than appending a section about this round.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/engineering.md` and `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.

After the repair, state its reach as repair_reach: a description of what you actually changed, never of how important the finding was. It is `contained` when the correction was structural with no behavioural difference — code moved, renamed or re-seamed while observable behaviour, contracts and schemas stay as they were — and the project's own deterministic checks over what you touched have been run and pass. It is `spreading` when behaviour, contracts, schemas, configuration, dependencies or generated output changed, or when those checks could not be run or did not pass. A repair that turned out larger than it looked is `spreading` whatever it looked like when you started, because `contained` skips the validation chain and returns straight to this gate — the checks that change could have invalidated would never run.
nodes.completionCondition: Repository content changed to repair reproduced architecture defects within the approved plan

nodes.directive:
The architecture review proves that the approved plan must change. Present what plan unit {{current_step_index}} completed, what remains, why the plan cannot be completed correctly, and how unfinished work would be carried forward. Ask whether the current unit may be closed for a new plan revision. Save the explicit decision and verbatim feedback to {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/closure-feedback.md. Do not revise the plan here.

In `autonomous` mode decide the closure yourself from the recorded architecture finding and the approved plan: close the current unit for a new revision only when the reviewed finding genuinely requires replanning rather than local repair. Do not ask the user.
nodes.completionCondition: The user explicitly approved or refused closure with durable feedback

nodes.directive:
Write the material plan revision {{plan_revision}} to {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{plan_revision}}/plan.md, from the previously approved plan at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{previous_plan_revision}}/plan.md and the actual completed work. Use whichever record drove this revision and exists: the architecture review of the current unit, the approved closure at {{workspace_path}}/plans/{{previous_plan_revision}}/closure-feedback.md, or the verbatim unit rejection at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/user-feedback.md. A revision reached through the replan teleport has none of them and must not wait for one. The engine has already advanced the revision number; do not renumber it. Preserve prior revisions, close only the unit whose closure was actually approved, carry every unfinished outcome into the next uncompleted units, and keep completed work immutable and executor tactics open.

Follow `{{workspace_path}}/standards/planning.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: The new material plan revision exists at its revision path, carries every unfinished outcome forward, and closes only a unit whose closure was actually approved

nodes.directive:
Determine runtime, browser, checklist, security, and performance applicability from canonical requirements, the approved plan unit, project policy, actual diff, changed/at-risk behavior inventory, and current evidence. Screenshot validation is applicable only when this exact approved plan unit explicitly requires screenshot capture, actual visual inspection, and step-report.html; incidental UI impact cannot enable it here. Execute every applicable project checklist item and record PASS with evidence, N/A with reason, or FAIL with location and correction. For applicable UI behavior, cover representative affected states and dependent behavior with project-native browser evidence. When screenshots are required, capture every required state, open the actual images with available visual capability, compare expected and observed behavior, and record the assessment; file existence alone is not evidence and unfinished capture/inspection means this directive is not complete. Write {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/runtime-validation.md with behavior-to-evidence mappings. Classify reproducible application or permanent project-native capture/tooling defects as repository_failure and unavailable external browser/vision infrastructure as external_blocker. Do not repeat deterministic checks that cannot diagnose runtime behavior.

Applicability and evidence belong to the unit as it now stands against its baseline, the line that opens {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md, not to the latest repair alone: re-establish the behaviour that change could have altered and keep the evidence it could not reach.
nodes.completionCondition: All applicable runtime and checklist work is complete; any required screenshots were captured, opened, and visually assessed; evidence and classification are truthful

nodes.directive:
Use the current runtime-validation report to reproduce and repair repository-caused runtime or specialized-check failures at their root. Change production code, tests, capture tooling, or documentation only as justified and preserve unrelated work. Never obtain a pass by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, visual expectations, security/performance gates, or another quality gate; change a validator or test only with concrete proof that it is obsolete. Do not add sleeps, force, blind retries, swallowed errors, suppression, or timeout inflation, and do not absorb unrelated or external failures. Record this correction in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/repair.md, the record of the round you are closing: what you changed, which earlier behaviour of the unit that could have disturbed, and the evidence for the repair itself, added to whatever an earlier correction of this same round already recorded, and run focused evidence before independent revalidation.

When this correction changed the unit, bring the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md to what the unit now is, in this same turn: you are its current owner, so rewrite what your change made untrue rather than appending a section about this round.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: Repository content changed to repair reproduced runtime defects

nodes.directive:
Present the concrete external blocker from the current runtime-validation report. Ask the user to confirm changed external state before retrying, or to abort. Do not retry unchanged.

In `autonomous` mode do not ask: re-check the external state yourself and retry only on evidence that it actually changed; otherwise abort with the blocker recorded.
nodes.completionCondition: The user confirmed changed state or chose abort

nodes.directive: After cheaper mutating and semantic gates have converged, decide whether a broad or expensive build, test, integration, runtime, or packaging check is required by project policy, affected contracts, or actual risk for plan unit {{current_step_index}}. The scope is the unit against its baseline, the line that opens {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md. Reuse equivalent current evidence when no later mutation can affect it; do not repeat a full suite mechanically on every iteration. Run applicable project-native checks and write {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/expensive-validation.md with exact commands and outcomes, evidence scope, or a concrete inapplicability reason. Classify reproducible repository failures separately from external blockers and never hide partial or failed results as pass.
nodes.completionCondition: Applicable non-stale expensive evidence or justified inapplicability exists with truthful classification

nodes.directive:
Use the current expensive-validation report to reproduce and repair every repository-caused failure at its root. Preserve unrelated work and do not broaden to unrelated or external failures. Never obtain a pass by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, build/integration gates, or another quality gate; change a validator or test only with concrete proof that it is obsolete. Do not add sleeps, force, blind retries, swallowed errors, suppression, or timeout inflation. Record this correction in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/iteration-{{current_iteration}}/repair.md, the record of the round you are closing: what you changed, which earlier behaviour of the unit that could have disturbed, and the evidence for the repair itself, added to whatever an earlier correction of this same round already recorded, and run focused evidence before returning through all stale cheaper and semantic gates.

When this correction changed the unit, bring the unit's account at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md to what the unit now is, in this same turn: you are its current owner, so rewrite what your change made untrue rather than appending a section about this round.

Repair against `{{workspace_path}}/standards/review.md`.
nodes.completionCondition: Repository content changed to repair reproduced expensive-validation failures

nodes.directive:
Present the concrete external blocker from the current expensive-validation report. Ask the user to confirm changed external state before retrying, or to abort. Do not retry unchanged.

In `autonomous` mode do not ask: re-check the external state yourself and retry only on evidence that it actually changed; otherwise abort with the blocker recorded.
nodes.completionCondition: The user confirmed changed state or chose abort

nodes.directive:
Determine from the approved plan, task authority, and material impact whether plan unit {{current_step_index}} requires user acceptance. If this exact approved unit requires screenshots and step-report.html, create or regenerate {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/step-report.html from the current stabilized implementation, runtime, screenshot, review, and expensive-validation evidence. Make it a portable self-contained HTML document with embedded styling and no external runtime dependency, responsive readability, explicit PASS/FAIL/warning states, factual language without marketing claims, and embedded images or reliable relative paths that remain valid from the documented location. State outcome, affected behavior, scenarios, commands/tests/reviews, limitations, expected versus observed screenshot assessments with honest baseline handling, and concise manual-verification instructions. Open or otherwise verify the final document and its image references, then present or link that exact report and request approval in the same substantive turn. Such a unit is never concluded without presenting it. If no visual-report obligation exists, do not create screenshot HTML; present concise behavior and exact verification evidence when user acceptance is materially required. Where acceptance is not materially required, conclude the unit yourself and record in {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/unit-report.md why it was not — the answer is the same `accepted` either way, because the run continues identically, and the reason belongs where its readers are. On rejection, also save verbatim feedback to {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/user-feedback.md. Do not repair here.

In `autonomous` mode do not wait for user acceptance: still create or regenerate the required step-report.html for units that carry a visual-report obligation, still record the evidence, and conclude the unit yourself with `accepted` so the run continues to the checkpoint decision. Reserve rejection for interactive runs.
nodes.completionCondition: The applicable acceptance decision and evidence are durable; required current HTML is presented and accepted or rejected; verbatim rejection feedback exists when needed

nodes.directive:
Use the verbatim plan-unit feedback at {{workspace_path}}/step-{{current_step_index}}/user-feedback.md and the current approved plan to resolve the rejection at its correct authority boundary. If feedback identifies an in-plan defect, reproduce and repair its root cause while preserving unrelated changes and without absorbing unrelated failures into task scope. Never obtain acceptance by weakening tests, assertions, schemas, types, lint, visual evidence, or another quality gate; change a validator or test only with concrete proof that it is obsolete. # Planning standards

These are outcomes, not procedures. An item that does not apply to the current change is met, and
nothing needs to be produced to prove it inapplicable. Cite only what is violated; do not walk this
document item by item.

## A unit is a vertical slice

Each unit changes observable behaviour and carries, inside itself, the tests and the verification
that prove it. It crosses whatever layers it needs to do that.

*Why.* A unit whose proof lives in a later unit cannot be accepted on its own, and nothing can tell
whether it is finished. Splitting by layer instead — one unit for storage, one for the API, one for
the interface — produces work that is neither independent nor separately valuable. (INVEST; vertical
vs horizontal slicing.)

## No unit is only tests, only validation, only documentation, or only cleanup

Unless that is what the task itself asks for.

*Why.* Such a unit is an admission that the previous one was delivered unfinished, and it moves the
proof away from the work it proves. The verification that ends up in a "testing" unit is the same
verification the implementing unit needed to be acceptable.

## The plan opens with the architecture it assumes

Components, how they interact, the decisions taken, and the consequences those decisions accept.
Decisions deliberately deferred are named as deferred.

*Why.* Without it the reviewer judges steps and never the shape, and the first unit silently fixes an
architecture nobody agreed to. Consequences are the part that makes the record useful later. (ADR:
context, decision, consequences.)

## Work moves from the core outward

Data and domain logic first, then integration and interfaces, then presentation — unless a real
dependency runs the other way and the plan says which.

*Why.* Building the outer layer first freezes a contract underneath it that nothing has exercised yet.

## Each unit is readable by someone who never saw the conversation

What it produces, what it depends on, and what evidence would show it done.

*Why.* The reviewer, and often the executor, arrive without that history; anything they cannot
reconstruct becomes an assumption nobody checks.

## The plan does not enumerate files, symbols, line numbers, or pseudocode

It fixes outcomes, contracts, invariants, dependencies, acceptance evidence, and known risks.

*Why.* Naming files before the code has been read chooses tactics blindly and substitutes a false
sense of completeness for the analysis the executor still has to do. The executor has the repository
in front of it; the planner does not. (INVEST — negotiable.)

## Size follows the work

One unit is a complete plan when the task is small. A unit that needs sub-items is two units.

*Why.* Padding a plan to look thorough adds review cycles without adding work, and sub-items hide a
unit that was never independently completable.

## Every unit names the evidence that would accept it

In observable terms: a behaviour to exercise, a state to inspect, an artifact to compare.

*Why.* Acceptance criteria written as adjectives — robust, clean, complete — cannot be met or
refused, so they end up decided by whoever is more insistent.

## Unresolved decisions are named as unresolved

*Why.* An open question recorded as an assumption becomes a defect that surfaces after the work is
built on top of it.

engineering_standards.default:
# Engineering standards

These are outcomes, not procedures. An item that does not apply to the current change is met, and
nothing needs to be produced to prove it inapplicable. Cite only what is violated; do not walk this
document item by item.

## A module hides a decision, and its interface is smaller than what it does

The interface is everything a caller must know: signatures, ordering constraints, error behaviour,
guarantees. Judge a module by how much complexity it removes from everyone else, not by its size.

*Why.* A module whose interface is nearly as complicated as its implementation has moved code
without hiding anything. Making a unit slightly larger to hide a decision is usually the better
trade. (Deep modules; information hiding.)

## The same design decision is not reflected in two places

Two modules that must both know a format, an ordering, or a schema are one decision leaked across a
boundary, and the boundary is in the wrong place.

*Why.* Leaked decisions change together and are found separately. The classic source is decomposing
by the order things happen rather than by the knowledge each part holds. (Information leakage;
temporal decomposition.)

## A published interface is extended or versioned, never quietly changed

Where callers exist outside the change, the old behaviour keeps working while the new one is
introduced, and the removal window is stated. Where callers are all inside the change, they are
updated in the same change.

*Why.* Consumers depend on every observable behaviour, documented or not, so "nobody uses that" is a
claim to verify, not to assume — and a version number alone communicates nothing to them. (Hyrum's
Law; empirical studies find breaking changes as often in minor releases as in major ones.)

## Dependencies point inward, and there are no cycles

Domain logic does not know about transport, storage, or presentation; the outer layers depend on it.

*Why.* When the core knows about the edge, the edge cannot be replaced or tested, and a cycle makes
both ends impossible to reason about alone.

## Abstraction appears after repetition, not before it

A second similar case is evidence; an anticipated third is not.

*Why.* An abstraction built for imagined cases fits none of them well, and its cost — the indirection
every reader now traverses — is paid immediately while the benefit stays hypothetical.

## Effects and state live at the edges

The core is deterministic and reachable by tests without infrastructure.

*Why.* Logic entangled with I/O can only be exercised through the slowest path available, so it stops
being exercised.

## Errors are handled where there is a decision to make

Context is preserved on the way up; failures are not swallowed, and are not converted into a success
value that a caller cannot distinguish.

*Why.* A caught error with nowhere to go becomes an invisible wrong result later, and the place that
could have decided has lost the information it needed.

## Data and schema changes carry a path forward and a path back

Migration, and what happens to data written by the previous shape.

*Why.* The failure appears in production, on data nobody has in development.

## Security and performance are stated with the contract they constrain

Not appended afterwards as a review topic.

*Why.* A constraint discovered after the interface exists is either ignored or forces the interface
to be rebuilt.

## Follow the project's patterns by analogy — and do not replicate a defect

Find the places that already solve this kind of problem and follow them. Where the surrounding code
is wrong, implement correctly, say plainly where you diverged and why, and report the defect you
found rather than silently repairing unrelated areas.

*Why.* Consistency is what makes a codebase readable, but consistency with a defect multiplies it,
and an unannounced divergence looks like an accident to the next reader. Repairing what the task did
not ask for hides the actual change inside unrelated diffs.

## What you touch does not get worse

Dead code, debug leftovers, and TODOs standing in for delivery are removed from what the change
touches.

*Why.* Each is a claim about the code that is no longer true, and the cost of verifying it falls on
every later reader.

test_standards.default:
# Test standards

These are outcomes, not procedures. An item that does not apply to the current change is met, and
nothing needs to be produced to prove it inapplicable. Cite only what is violated; do not walk this
document item by item.

## A test names the behaviour it protects and fails when that behaviour regresses

If no realistic defect makes it fail, it is not protecting anything.

*Why.* This is the property every other one serves: a suite that cannot fail for a behavioural reason
reports churn instead of regressions. (Test Desiderata — behavioural.)

## Tests exercise the public surface and assert state, not interactions

Reach the behaviour the way a caller reaches it. Assert what the system ends up being or returning,
not which internal calls happened in which order.

*Why.* Asserting interactions couples the test to the current implementation, so it fails on every
refactor that changes nothing observable — the change-detector test — and, worse, keeps passing when
a collaborator's real behaviour changes underneath. (Google: change-detector tests; test state, not
interactions.)

## A test does not assert what the compiler, type system, or linter already guarantees

That a field exists, that an argument has a type, that formatting holds.

*Why.* Such an assertion cannot fail for a behavioural reason — the earlier tool fails first — so it
adds maintenance without adding protection, and it makes the suite look stronger than it is. This
one is reasoning from the properties above rather than a citation; the literature names the adjacent
case, a test that re-implements the production algorithm to compare it with itself.

## No assertion that cannot fail, and none that might not run

An assertion inside a conditional the run may skip, a test with no assertion at all, or an expectation
that restates its input.

*Why.* All three report success without having checked anything, and they are indistinguishable from
real coverage in every report the project produces.

## Each level asserts its own responsibility

Unit for logic and boundaries, integration for the contract between components, end-to-end for the
user-visible path. The same behaviour is not asserted at three levels.

*Why.* Duplicated assertions multiply the cost of every change to that behaviour, and when they
disagree nobody knows which one states the intent.

## Tests are deterministic and independent of order

No dependence on wall-clock time, network, shared mutable state, or on another test having run first.

*Why.* A test that fails intermittently trains everyone to rerun rather than investigate, and it
takes real failures down with it. (Test Desiderata — isolated, deterministic.)

## A performance assertion carries a threshold that can fail

*Why.* A measurement without a bound records a number; it never reports a regression.

## The name states the condition and the expected outcome

Not the method under test.

*Why.* When it fails, the name is the whole diagnosis a reader gets before opening anything.

## Fixtures and helpers come from the project

Use the existing helpers, factories, and auth or setup utilities rather than building a parallel set.

*Why.* Parallel infrastructure drifts from the real setup, and its tests then pass against a world
the application does not live in.

## A defect is closed by a test that failed before the fix

*Why.* Otherwise nothing proves the fix addressed the reported behaviour, and the same defect can
return unnoticed.

## Coverage artifacts the project maintains are updated with the change

*Why.* A coverage map nobody updates stops describing the suite and starts misleading the next
author. Coverage percentage itself is not a quality criterion: it records that lines executed, not
that behaviour was checked. (SWE at Google, testing overview.)

documentation_standards.default:
# Documentation standards

These are outcomes, not procedures. An item that does not apply to the current change is met, and
nothing needs to be produced to prove it inapplicable. Cite only what is violated; do not walk this
document item by item.

## Documentation describes the current state

No change history, no "previously", no announcements of what is new, no promises about what will
come.

*Why.* A reader arrives to learn how the system behaves now. History in a reference page makes them
reconstruct which sentence is still true, and the version control system already holds the history
properly.

## Every claim is checkable against the code, the configuration, or a command that runs

Examples work as written; commands are the ones the project actually has.

*Why.* One example that fails costs more trust than ten missing pages, and readers cannot tell a
stale example from a mistake of their own.

## Each page has one job

Teaching a newcomer, guiding someone through a task, stating facts to look up, or explaining why the
design is what it is. Knowing which one a page is tells you what belongs in it and what belongs
elsewhere.

*Why.* A page that mixes them serves nobody: the learner drowns in reference detail and the person
looking up a fact wades through narrative. This is a discipline for the author, not a required
directory layout — projects adopt it incrementally. (Diátaxis.)

## What is documented is the contract and the behaviour

Internal detail appears only where a reader must act on it.

*Why.* Documented internals become promises: readers depend on them, and changing them then breaks
people who followed the documentation.

## Placement and form follow the project

Match the structure, depth, and voice of the documentation that already exists; project style comes
first, house style second.

*Why.* Documentation is read as a set, not as pages; a page in a foreign format reads as an
afterthought regardless of its content. Style guides are guidance and yield to project style.
(Google developer documentation style guide.)

## Translations stay in parity where the project keeps more than one language

The same pages, the same structure, the same claims; a change lands in all of them or in none.

*Why.* A partially updated translation is worse than an untranslated one, because it states outdated
facts with the same authority as current ones.

## No new long-lived document without a durable reader

Update the page that already owns the subject.

*Why.* Documents accumulate faster than they are read; each new one splits the subject and makes the
next author guess which is authoritative.

## No numbers that drift

Counts of tests, tools, node types, or packages.

*Why.* They are wrong within weeks and nothing fails when they are, so they teach readers to distrust
the rest of the page.

review_standards.default:
# Review, repair, and evidence

These are outcomes, not procedures. An item that does not apply to the current change is met, and
nothing needs to be produced to prove it inapplicable. Cite only what is violated; do not walk this
document item by item.

## Review

### Independence is required where the flow marks a review independent

Where a review is declared independent, whoever produced the artifact does not review it: a subagent
or a separate context is the usual way to obtain that, and where no such context is available, say so
plainly in the report rather than pretending the review was independent.

Where a flow judges a gate locally — the same agent, in the ordinary run — the obligation is
different and just as binding: judge from the primary sources rather than from your own account of
the work, and do not lower the bar because you wrote the thing. Do not manufacture independence a
local gate did not ask for; delegation costs a turn and a context, and the flow decides where to
spend it.

*Why.* The producer knows what they meant, so they read the intent instead of the artifact — which is
exactly the failure the review exists to catch. Reading the diff, the tests and the evidence instead
of your memory is what recovers most of that at a local gate; a flow buys a genuinely separate reader
where the risk justifies the cost.

### The reviewer reads the primary sources

The actual artifact, the requirements it answers to, the surrounding code — not the producer's
account of what it does.

*Why.* A summary carries the producer's assumptions forward, including the one that caused the defect.

### The subject is the unit's current state, not the round's increment

A gate judges what the unit is now, measured against the state the unit started from — not the diff
of the latest repair. A defect the current round did not introduce is still a defect of the unit.

*Why.* By the fifth round the latest diff is three lines, and judging those three lines passes a unit
whose rounds broke each other's work. Judging the increment also leaves a regression homeless: the
round that caused it is over, so no later gate owns it.

### The baseline the unit is judged against is stated once and reused

It is the previous unit's checkpoint where the project's version control provides one, otherwise the
state recorded when the unit began. Whichever it is, the unit's first iteration writes it down in a
line, and everything afterwards refers to that line.

*Why.* With no written baseline each reviewer picks its own, and the ones that pick the last
iteration are judging the increment while believing they judge the unit.

### Each round is judged on its own

Re-read the artifact instead of inheriting a conclusion from the previous round, including your own.
"This was fine last time" is not evidence that it is fine now.

*Why.* Carried-forward conclusions accumulate: what was checked in the first round is an assumption
by the fourth, and the repair that invalidated it is exactly the change nobody re-examined.

### The report holds the complete current set of confirmed findings

One known file, overwritten each time. Each finding gives its location, the contract it violates, the
consequence that follows, and what would resolve it. Outward, only the count the routing needs.

*Why.* Findings revealed one per round turn a repair into a queue of surprises, and findings copied
into workflow context drift from the file that holds them.

### Zero findings is a valid and expected outcome

A reviewer that must produce something will find a naming preference.

*Why.* The reviewer's job is to decide whether the artifact is acceptable, and a search that continues
until something is found makes the loop about the reviewer rather than the work. (Google's reviewer
standard.)

### Blocking requires an observable consequence

Something must break, be lost, be unverifiable, or violate a stated requirement. Style, naming,
speculative robustness, and hypothetical future needs are worth saying and are not blocking; say so
when you raise them.

*Why.* The standard is that the change definitely improves the state of the system, not that it is
perfect — nothing worsens the system's health, and nothing waits for polish. Technical facts overrule
preferences, and where no rule exists, existing code wins over taste. (Google: improvement, not
perfection; the "Nit:" convention.)

### The reviewer diagnoses the work; it does not repair it and does not design machinery

No new fields, protocols, or layers proposed for robustness nobody asked for. The one thing a
reviewer may change is the run's own record, under the rule below.

*Why.* A reviewer that rewrites the artifact is no longer independent of it, and a reviewer that
designs is proposing work instead of proving a defect.

### A finding is about the delivered work, not about the run's bookkeeping

A finding names something wrong in what is being delivered: the code, the tests, the documentation the
project keeps, or the evidence that the work is what it claims to be. The reports, reviews and
accounts a run writes into its own workspace are not the delivery.

The question that separates the two is whether editing the record alone makes its statement true.
When it does — a number that no longer matches the tree, a paragraph left standing after the change it
described was undone — whoever notices corrects that file where it stands, says so in their own
report, and raises no finding. When it does not, because the statement can only be made true by
changing the repository, it is a finding like any other: a record claiming work that was never done
hides work that was never done.

A reader whose role is to judge the delivery corrects records and never touches the repository; that
boundary is what keeps it independent of what it judges.

*Why.* A stale record is a two-line edit, and routing it as a finding buys the whole validation chain
for it — the cost that teaches a run to batch findings and an author to delete gates. What the record
protects is the reader who comes next, and that reader is served by the correction plus a sentence
saying it was wrong, not by a repair round.

### A delegated reviewer does not repeat mechanical checks whose evidence is current

Linters, type checks, test suites, and builds have already run.

*Why.* Rerunning them consumes the review turn on evidence that already exists and displaces the
judgement only a reviewer can supply.

## Repair

### The repair owner reproduces the defect before changing anything

*Why.* A fix aimed at a finding nobody reproduced usually changes something adjacent and leaves the
defect in place.

### A finding that cannot be reproduced is reported as such

With what was tried. It is not silently closed, and it does not start another identical round.

*Why.* An unchanged repeat costs a full cycle and produces the same report; the disagreement between
reviewer and repair owner is the actual finding at that point.

### The changed artifact returns to the same reviewer

*Why.* A second reviewer re-derives the context and finds a different set, so nothing ever converges.

## Evidence

### Evidence is what another person can reproduce

A command and its output, an inspected artifact, an observed state. Not a claim that something works.

*Why.* "Verified" without a trace is indistinguishable from unverified, and the run that has to be
resumed later cannot tell them apart either.

### A report states what the work delivers, not how much of it there was

The subject of a report is the outcome and the evidence for it. A number belongs in it when the
number is the deliverable, or is itself the output of a check that can fail — a test run, the count
of source remarks closed, a revision identifier. A number that measures the volume of the work —
files touched, lines added or removed, share of comment, percent reduced — is neither, and it is not
written.

*Why.* Reproducibility makes size the easiest number to produce, and nothing fails when a size number
drifts, so nothing keeps it true. Written down it is still a claim: the reviewer has to verify it and
the repair owner has to maintain it, which spends a round of review and a round of repair on a figure
that protects nothing.

### The account of the work is kept current by whoever last changed the work

Where a flow keeps a durable account of what the work now delivers, that account has one address, and
the responsibility that last changed the work leaves it true in the same turn. It is rewritten to
describe the present state, not appended to with the history of the rounds — the record of a round
is the round's own report.

*Why.* Gates and reviewers judge the current state. An account frozen at the first round disagrees
with the artifact by construction, and the disagreement surfaces as a review finding, so the round is
spent reconciling a description instead of judging the work.

### A change makes stale the evidence covering what it could have touched

That surface is re-established; evidence the change could not reach stays current, and which is which
is said rather than assumed. Deliberate before-and-after comparison keeps the earlier evidence on
purpose — that is not staleness.

*Why.* Treating every repair as invalidating everything makes each round cost a full revalidation,
which is how gates start being skipped wholesale; treating nothing as invalidated ships a unit whose
last change was never checked.

### An artifact's existence is not evidence it was inspected

Where visual acceptance matters, the images are opened and compared against expected behaviour; a
file on disk proves only that a file was produced.

*Why.* Capture that nobody looked at reliably passes while showing the wrong screen.

### An inapplicable check is recorded as inapplicable, with the reason

It is neither silently skipped nor reported as passed.

*Why.* A skipped check that reads as green is the one nobody revisits when the situation changes.

### Partial and failed results are reported as partial and failed

*Why.* A run reported as green on partial evidence moves the discovery of the failure to whoever
depends on it next, with less context than you have now.
